***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

Smectymnuus

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

Smectymnuus

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

Smectymnuus

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

Smectymnuus

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

Smectymnuus

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

Smectymnuus

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

Smectymnuus

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

- Complete the TASK by only using the available TOOLS.

- A CYCLE is specified through a Thought-Act-Observe pattern.

- A LOOP is a sequence of CYCLES that is used to finish a TASK.
- Once the LOOP is finished you MUST call `final_answer` to report the result.

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

Smectymnuus

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England \"Church of England\"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly \"Westminster Assembly\"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.\\n\\nThe name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) \"Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)\"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder \"Edmund Calamy the Elder\"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen \"Matthew Newcomen\"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow \"William Spurstow\"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall\\'s](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton \"John Milton\") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus\\'s reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)\\n\\nThis response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.\\n\\nMilton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions \"Animadversions\")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus \"Apology for Smectymnuus\")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n1. They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. ***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

Smectymnuus

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](./Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](./Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](./Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](./Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](./Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](./William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](./Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](./Smectymnuus#cite_note-3)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](./Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

The *[Apology](./Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](./Milton's_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-9)

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](./Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](./Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](./England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](./Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-6)\\n\\nThemes\\n------\\n\\nThe *Apology*, like many of Milton\\'s other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual\\'s character.[[4]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how \"Milton\\'s self is produced in the process of writing\" and that his self is put through \"a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations\".[[8]](./Apology_for_Smectymnuus#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains \"Milton\\'s understanding of [Aristotle](./Aristotle \"Aristotle\")\\'s definition of man as a political animal.
